title: The call of the king
hookLine: a good king's call, heard first, and then Christ's
last: WHAT HAVE I DONE FOR CHRIST.

lines: SAME FOOD, SAME WORK, SAME NIGHTS.
cards: A recruiting speech, and an unusual one. A king stands before his people and says: come with me. You'll eat what I eat, wear what I wear, work with me by day and keep watch with me by night.
Share the hard part, and you'll share the victory. Just: with me. Ignatius had been a soldier before his conversion, and this page of the Exercises sounds like it.
He asks the person praying to hear that speech, and to notice how any decent person would answer. Then he turns the page.

teach.h: A KING WHO SHARES THE HARD PART.
teach.b: The call of the king stands at the doorway of the second week, and it works like a parable in two steps. First, a human king.
Ignatius pictures a leader chosen by God, good and just, calling people in the terms of his own century to a hard campaign. The campaign isn't the point. The way he calls is.
No orders from a safe distance. Same food, same clothes, same nights. Ignatius says it would be shameful to hear a call like that and hang back.
Step two: if that's how we'd answer a good human leader, how much more Christ. Now the king is Christ our Lord, and the call goes out to every person.
His aim, as Ignatius puts it, is to bring the whole world to his Father, and whoever wants to come must labor with him, so that following him in the pain, they may follow him in the glory.
By the Sea of Galilee, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says to two fishermen: "Come ye after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men."
Then Ignatius notices two kinds of answer.

teach.h: WHO WALKS INTO THE WORK FIRST?
teach.b: Anyone with judgment and reason, he says, will offer themselves for the work.
Some will want to go further: to follow even into poverty and insult, if that is what Christ chooses for them. The Exercises leave that further offering to the person's freedom.
And the meditation leaves a plain question about anyone who calls you: do they send you into the work, or walk into it first?

how: In an Ignatian retreat, the meditation on the call of the king is prayed before the second week begins, as a way of asking how fully the person wants to follow Christ.

games.q: what does “the call of the king” mean?
o: a good king's call that points to Christ's call
a royal decree calling Spain's knights to arms
the speech Ignatius gave when founding the Jesuits

games.q: the call of the king — tap the pairs.
p: same food, same clothes, same nights

s: Ignatius's king gives orders from a safe distance
he eats, dresses, works and keeps watch with his people. that's the whole argument.
the human king's call is there to help hear Christ's call
if we'd answer a good human leader, how much more Christ.
Ignatius requires everyone to offer poverty and insult
anyone with judgment, he says, will offer themselves for the work. going further is left to each person's freedom.

games.q: a good king says: come with me. you'll eat what I eat and keep watch when I keep watch. what does Ignatius say a decent person does?
o: wait to see whether the campaign succeeds.
send someone else in your place.
games.why: Ignatius says it would be shameful to hear a call like that and hang back. then he turns it to Christ: how much more.

practice: Hear the call in its shortest form: come after me. If you pray, answer Christ in your own words, or with today's line, I want to follow, and let one place for tomorrow come to mind: a kitchen, a desk.
If you don't pray, think of someone you'd follow because they worked right beside you, and ask what made the difference.

wordCard.voice: The call of the king. A good king's call, heard first, so that Christ's call can be heard more clearly. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek of Matthew 4:19: come, after me. the call to the fishermen.

carryVoice: Your line: I want to follow. Same food, same work, same nights. Same time tomorrow.
